cover.headline: Sample Story: A Port City Moves Its Trucks to the Night
paragraphs: This is fictional test content. In the sample city of Port Marlow, officials have decided to **roll out** dedicated night lanes for freight trucks, hoping to clear the daytime roads that drivers have complained about for years.

The plan is simple on paper. From ten at night until five in the morning, two lanes on the main harbour road will be reserved for heavy vehicles. During the day, the same lanes will return to buses, cars and motorbikes. City planners say the change could remove hundreds of trucks from rush-hour traffic every day.

For years, the harbour road has been the city's worst **bottleneck**. Ships arrive at all hours, but most warehouses only accept goods during office time. As a result, trucks queue in the morning and block the road just as office workers are trying to reach their desks. Local businesses say the delays have a __significant__ cost, because late deliveries mean empty shelves and unhappy customers.

To make the night lanes work, the city is offering an **incentive** to warehouses that open after dark. Companies that stay open at night will pay lower fees at the port for the first two years. Several large firms have already agreed to take part, while smaller ones say they need more time to hire night staff.

Not everyone is convinced. Residents who live near the harbour worry about noise from engines and brakes in the middle of the night. Some drivers' groups also point out that night shifts are tiring and can be unsafe if workers do not get enough rest. The city has promised to measure noise levels and to limit the speed of trucks in residential areas.

Experts say the idea is not new. Several cities have tried to spread deliveries across the day, with mixed results. The key, they argue, is cooperation. If ports, warehouses and shops all change their hours together, the night lanes can ease traffic. If only one group changes, trucks may simply wait somewhere else.

Why does this matter beyond one sample city? Many fast-growing cities, including Bangkok, face the same problem: roads designed for fewer vehicles now carry far more goods. Online shopping has added millions of small deliveries. Moving some of that traffic to quieter hours is one of the cheapest ways to make roads work better, because it uses space that already exists.

City officials say they will review the scheme after six months. If traffic improves and complaints stay low, the night lanes could become permanent. If not, the city says it will look for a different __approach__, such as new rail links to the port. For now, residents will watch closely to see whether their morning trip becomes a little easier.

world.headline: Sample Story: Coastal Towns Share E-Bikes
paragraphs: This is fictional test content. Three small coastal towns have started a shared e-bike network. Residents can rent a bike in one town and return it in another. The towns are connected by a flat coastal path, so the trip is easy for most people.

Local leaders say the network should help people who work in a neighbouring town and have no car. Buses between the towns are slow and do not run late. An e-bike makes the **commute** faster and cheaper, they say.
The project is also part of a plan to cut traffic in the summer, when many tourists visit. Officials hope visitors will use the bikes instead of driving between beaches.
The towns will check how many people use the bikes each month. If the numbers are good, they plan to add more bikes and two new stations next year.

world.headline: Sample Story: New Rules for Delivery Apps
paragraphs: This is fictional test content. Regulators in a sample country are reviewing the rules for food-delivery apps. The apps have grown very fast, and many riders say they do not know how their pay is calculated.
The review follows months of public **scrutiny**. Riders' groups have asked for clearer pay rules and better insurance. Restaurant owners have also complained about high fees.

The regulators say they want to __ensure__ that riders understand their income before they accept a job. One idea is to show the full payment on the screen before each order. Another is to require basic accident insurance for every rider.

The delivery companies say they support fair rules. However, they warn that higher costs could mean higher prices for customers. A first draft of the new rules is expected early next year, and the public will be able to comment on it.

thailand.headline: Sample Story: More Evening Boats on the Canal
paragraphs: This is fictional test content. A commuter boat line in Bangkok will add evening trips from next month. The boats travel along a khlong, a canal that runs through the city, and many office workers use them to avoid traffic.
Passengers have asked for later boats for a long time. At the moment, the last boat leaves before many offices close, so some workers must take a taxi or a motorcycle taxi home.
The operator says the extra trips will make the service more **sustainable** because more people will use it every day. It will also add two new piers.
The operator plans to check passenger numbers after three months. If the evening boats are popular, it may also add weekend trips.

thailand.headline: Sample Story: Farmers Test Drought-Tolerant Rice
paragraphs: This is fictional test content. Farmers in a northern province are testing a new type of rice that needs less water. The trial is part of a programme to help farmers during dry years.
Many farmers in the area depend on rain. When the rainy season starts late, their young rice plants can die. The new rice can survive longer without water, so the risk is lower.
Some farmers are **reluctant** to change, because they know their old rice well and trust it. Others say they are ready to try anything that reduces their losses.
Officials will compare the harvest from the new rice with the usual rice at the end of the season. If the results are good, more seeds will be offered to farmers next year.

feature_a.headline: Your Phone Knows When You Commute. Should It?
paragraphs: Most smartphones quietly learn our daily habits. They notice when we leave home, which route we take and when we usually arrive at work. With this information, the phone can show the traffic before we ask, or remind us to leave early when the roads are busy.

For many people, this feels helpful. A phone that predicts your **commute** can save time and stress, especially in a city with heavy traffic. Map apps can suggest a faster route, and calendar apps can warn you that you will be late for a meeting.

However, the same data can reveal a lot about you. A record of where you go every day shows where you live, where you work and even where you spend your free time. If that data is shared with other companies, it could be used for advertising or sold to third parties.

The good news is that you can control much of it. Both major phone systems let you see which apps use your location. You can choose to share your location only while an app is open, or not at all. You can also delete your location history and turn off features that you do not use.

A sensible __approach__ is to review your settings every few months. Ask yourself a simple question for each app: does it really need to know where I am? A taxi app needs your location to pick you up. A torch app does not.
Technology can make daily life easier, but it works best when we understand the deal we are making. A few minutes in your settings can give you the benefits without giving away more than you want.

feature_b.headline: Why We Queue: Small Habits That Shape a Culture
paragraphs: Visitors to Bangkok often notice how people line up neatly at train platforms, following arrows painted on the floor. The habit seems small, but it says a lot about how a city shares limited space.

Queuing is a kind of silent agreement. Everyone accepts a small delay so that the whole group moves smoothly. When the agreement works, nobody needs to give orders. When it breaks down, even a short wait can feel stressful and unfair.

Different cultures have different queuing styles. In some places, a queue is a straight line and cutting in is a serious offence. In others, a queue is more like a crowd, and people move forward when they see a gap. Neither style is wrong, but visitors can feel confused when the local rules are not written down.

Design plays a big role. Floor markings, barriers and clear signs make the right behaviour obvious. Train stations that mark where the doors will open help passengers wait at the side, so people getting off can leave quickly. Small details like these have a real __impact__ on how calm a busy place feels.

Technology is changing the queue too. Many restaurants and clinics now give customers a number by text message, so they can wait somewhere comfortable instead of standing in line. Some people love this, while others miss the clear feeling of a real line.
Next time you join a queue, notice its rules. Who stands where? How close do people stand? What happens if someone cuts in? These small moments are a quiet lesson in the culture around you.

two_takes.question: Should offices stop serving free snacks?

view_a.title: Yes: Free snacks cost more than they seem
view_a.text: Free snacks look like a small perk, but they can be expensive for a company, especially a young one. Admittedly, staff enjoy them, and a bowl of fruit can make an office feel friendly. However, many snacks are sweet and salty, which does not help anyone's health. Companies that want to **cut back on** costs could spend the same money on things that matter more, such as training or better chairs. It seems fair to say that a good workplace is built on clear goals and respect, not on biscuits. Staff can still bring their own food, and teams can share treats on special days.

view_b.title: No: Small comforts build a team
view_b.text: It is true that snacks cost money, but the amount is usually small compared with salaries. On the other hand, a shared snack table gives people a reason to stop and talk. Those short chats often lead to useful ideas and stronger teams. Snacks can arguably also save time, because staff do not need to leave the building when they feel hungry in the afternoon. If health is the worry, the answer is simple: offer fruit, nuts and yoghurt instead of cakes. Removing snacks completely may send the message that the company does not value small comforts.

trap.title: Arrive at or arrive to?
trap.wrong: I arrived to the office at eight.
trap.right: I arrived at the office at eight.
trap.explanation: Thai speakers often think of ถึง as 'to', so they say 'arrive to'. In English we arrive at a building or point, arrive in a city or country, and never arrive to a place.

other_language.headline: German: Punctuality Is a Form of Respect
other_language.note: In Germany, being on time is more than good manners. Many people see it as a sign that you respect other people's time. Trains are expected to run to the minute, and a meeting that starts at nine really starts at nine. If you will be even five minutes late, it is polite to send a message. Germans also tend to separate work time and free time clearly, so after-hours emails may not get a quick reply.
